elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract text explicitly calls the report a 'living systematic review', identifying it as a systematic review.

elements.quote: randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objective/review question: to compare effects of all treatment interventions for COVID-19 across age groups.

elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main inclusion criterion (randomized clinical trials of treatment interventions for participants with COVID-19 across all age groups); this constitutes reporting of primary inclusion criteria.

elements.quote: Wesearched relevant databases and websites for published and unpublished trials until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract reports when searches were done (until August 7, 2020) but only refers generically to 'relevant databases and websites' rather than identifying the specific information sources used.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed trial methodology.
elements.reason: The abstract states that two reviewers independently assessed trial methodology, but it does not name the specific risk-of-bias tool or detailed methods used to assess risk of bias in the included studies.

elements.quote: We planned to conduct aggregate data meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses, network meta-analysis, and individual patient data meta-analyses. We performed both fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the methods planned and used to present and synthesize results, including types of meta-analyses and use of fixed-effect and random-effects models.

elements.quote: We included 33 randomized clinical trials enrolling a total of 13,312 participants.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and total participants and provides summary characteristics (e.g., all trials at high risk of bias).

elements.quote: This trial showed evidence of a beneficial effect of dexamethasone on all-cause mortality (rate ratio 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75-0.93; p < 0.001; low certainty) and on mechanical ventilation (risk ratio [RR] 0.77; 95% CI 0.62-0.95; p = 0.021; low certainty). ... Meta-analysis showed no evidence of a difference between remdesivir versus placebo on all-cause mortality (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.40-1.37; p = 0.34, I2 = 58%; 2 trials; very low certainty) ... Meta-analysis showed evidence of a beneficial effect of remdesivir versus placebo on serious adverse events (RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.63-0.94; p = 0.009, I2 = 0%; 2 trials; very low certainty).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes, including effect estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, and counts of trials/participants for specific outcomes.

elements.quote: This trial showed evidence of a beneficial effect of dexamethasone on all-cause mortality (rate ratio 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75-0.93; p < 0.001; low certainty) ... Meta-analysis showed no evidence of a difference between remdesivir versus placebo on all-cause mortality (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.40-1.37; p = 0.34, I2 = 58%; 2 trials; very low certainty).
elements.reason: Where meta-analyses were conducted, the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals for main outcomes.

elements.quote: This trial showed evidence of a beneficial effect of dexamethasone on all-cause mortality ... Meta-analysis showed evidence of a harmful effect on nonserious adverse events (RR 2.40; 95% CI 2.01-2.87; p < 0.00001; I2 = 90%; 6 trials; very low certainty).
elements.reason: The abstract indicates direction of effects (beneficial or harmful) and which intervention is favored for key comparisons.

elements.quote: All trials were at overall high risk of bias. ... The main limitation of this living review is the paucity of data currently available. Furthermore, the included trials were all at risks of systematic errors and random errors.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes important limitations of the included evidence, specifically high risk of bias and paucity of data (imprecision and risk of systematic/random errors).

elements.quote: Our study showed that dexamethasone and remdesivir might be beneficial for COVID-19 patients, but the certainty of the evidence was low to very low, so more trials are needed.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides a general interpretation of results and their implications (potential benefit of certain treatments but low certainty, need for more trials).

elements.quote: Funding: SJ, JCJ, and CG received a grant from The Grundfos Foundation (Grant number: 2020025, URL: https://www.pdjf.dk/en/). NN received a grant from The Swedish Research Council ... AAV received a European Union's Horizon 2020 grant (Grant number: 754936). The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.
elements.reason: The abstract (Methods and Findings section) includes the funding sources and grant numbers for the review authors.

No evidence in the provided abstract text explicitly gives the registration name and registration number; the PROSPERO registration (CRD42020178787) appears in the Methods section (text_8) but is not shown as included in the abstract content provided.

elements.quote: No evidence-based treatment for COVID-19 currently exist to augment widely used supportive care protocols [7]. To control the growing COVID-19 pandemic, we rely on quarantine, isolation, and infection-control measures to prevent disease spread [7] and on supportive care, including oxygen and mechanical ventilation, for infected patients. Many randomized clinical trials assessing the effects of different potential treatments for COVID-19 are currently underway.
elements.reason: Describes current state (no evidence-based treatments, reliance on supportive care and public health measures) and uncertainties (many trials underway indicating unanswered questions).

elements.quote: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection has spread rapidly worldwide, causing an international outbreak of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: Explains the importance and need for the review (rapid global spread and explicit statement of need for a living systematic review to evaluate interventions).

elements.quote: Wehave identified 4 important reviews that are comparable to our present project [77-80]. The first is a network meta-analysis just published in BMJ [77]. However, at the time of publication, this project did not include all relevant trials [50,52,54-56,59-61,64], including the pivotal trials assessing the effects of hydroxychloroquine [54,55,59]. The second project is a literature review published in JAMA ... Moreover, this review was only a narrative review without meta-analytic methods and trial sequential analysis [78]. The third project is a living mapping of ongoing randomized clinical trials with network meta-analysis on all interventions for COVID-19. ... This review includes both prevention and treatment and does not use trial sequential analysis or similar methods to handle problems with multiplicity ... The fourth project is a preprint of a rapid review ... These studies included patients with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS, n = 33), Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS, n = 16), COVID-19 ( n = 3), and unspecified coronavirus (n = 2). ... The authors conclude that current evidence for the effectiveness and safety of antiviral therapies for COVID-19 is inconclusive and suffers from a lack of well-designed prospective trials. Moreover, this review was only a narrative review without meta-analytic methods and trial sequential analysis [9].
elements.reason: Identifies and cites existing comparable reviews and explains differences/limitations of those reviews, justifying the need for the current review.

No retrieved evidence describes proposed mechanisms of action of the interventions assessed; the text focuses on disease spectrum, lack of treatments, and trial evidence rather than intervention mechanisms.
No retrieved evidence presents or refers to a logic model for complex interventions or delivery contexts; nothing in the provided text indicates a logic model was considered.

elements.quote: There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the objective to evaluate beneficial and harmful effects of interventions for COVID-19, but it does not present the objectives in a question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO) or as a clearly structured research question.

No explicit planned comparisons framed using PICO (population, intervention, comparator, outcome) or an appropriate variant are provided in the retrieved evidence; outcomes are listed but specific PICO-style planned comparisons are not reported.

elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies eligible study design (randomized clinical trials) and participant populations (all age groups). It also indicates outcomes and that trial results at maximum follow-up were used (text_13). However, it does not fully specify other study characteristics such as settings (e.g., inpatient vs outpatient) or explicit follow-up duration requirements, so the eligibility characteristics are incompletely reported.

elements.quote: Trials were included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year, and publication type.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states eligibility criteria for report characteristics (language, publication status, year, and type).

No explicit statement distinguishes exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported. The closest note describes one trial "not eligible for meta-analysis, as the results were not reported in a usable way" (text_22), but this does not constitute a general policy distinguishing the two reasons.

elements.quote: We identified 8 trials comparing hydroxychloroquine added to standard care versus standard care alone [35,36,43,49,55,56,59,60]. We also identified one trial that used placebo as an additional control intervention [54].
elements.reason: The review reports specific groups and comparisons used in syntheses (examples include hydroxychloroquine vs standard care, remdesivir vs placebo as noted elsewhere), indicating how some syntheses were grouped. However, it does not comprehensively present all groupings used in each synthesis or explicitly link each synthesis grouping to the comparisons defined in the review objectives, so reporting is incomplete.

No explicit rationales are provided for notable restrictions on study eligibility (for example, the choice to include only randomized trials is not accompanied by an explicit rationale in the supplied evidence).

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: A date (August 7, 2020) is reported for the electronic database searches collectively, but last-search dates are not reported for other information sources (trial registries, websites, preprint servers, etc.).

elements.quote: An information specialist searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE Ovid), Excerpta Medica database (Embase Ovid), Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS; Bireme), Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED; Web of Science), Conference Proceedings Citation Index-Science (CPCI-S; Web of Science), BIOSIS (Web of Science), CINAHL (EBSCO host), Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), China Network Knowledge Information (CNKI), Chinese Science Journal Database (VIP), and Wafang Database to identify relevant trials. We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: Names of many bibliographic databases and some platforms/search interfaces (e.g., MEDLINE Ovid, Embase Ovid, CINAHL (EBSCO host), CENTRAL in The Cochrane Library, Web of Science indices) are reported and coverage is stated as 'from their inception' to Aug 7, 2020; however, a platform or interface is not specified for every listed database (e.g., Wafang) and per-source coverage details are not given individually.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) of Europe, USA, and China, and websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). We also searched the COVID-19 Study Registry [13] and the real-time dashboard of randomized trials [14].
elements.reason: Names of several trial registers and registries are provided, but no information on any date restrictions or the last-search dates specific to these registers is reported.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched ... websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). We also searched the COVID-19 Study Registry [13] and the real-time dashboard of randomized trials [14]. We also searched preprint servers (bioRxiv, medRxiv) for unpublished trials.
elements.reason: Several websites and online sources (FDA, EMA, COVID-19 Study Registry, real-time dashboard, bioRxiv, medRxiv) are named, but explicit URLs are not provided for these sources and full search-method details for each online source/URL are not reported.

elements.quote: To identify unpublished trials, we searched ... websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). ... We contacted all trial authors to obtain individual patient data.
elements.reason: The authors report searching websites of pharmaceutical companies and regulatory bodies (FDA, EMA) and state they contacted all trial authors, but do not name specific organisations or manufacturers that were contacted to identify studies.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted are specified (trial authors).

elements.quote: The reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked for any unidentified randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The authors specify that they examined reference lists of relevant trial publications.

elements.quote: The reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked for any unidentified randomized clinical trials.
elements.reason: The report describes checking reference lists but does not report performing backward or forward citation searching (no seed reports, citation index/platform, or citation search dates are provided); thus this specific item (detailed backward/forward citation searching) does not apply based on the presented methods.

elements.quote: An information specialist searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, ... Conference Proceedings Citation Index-Science (CPCI-S; Web of Science) ... We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: Conference proceedings/index (CPCI-S) is named as searched and coverage period for databases including this index is stated ('from their inception' to Aug 7, 2020), meeting the requirement to report journals/conference proceedings source names and dates covered.

elements.quote: For the detailed search strategies for all electronic searches, see S2 Text.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly directs readers to S2 Text for the detailed search strategies for all electronic searches, indicating the complete strategies are provided in the supplementary material.

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020. Trials were included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year, and publication type.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the search limits (time frame and lack of language/publication restrictions) but does not explicitly justify these choices by reference to the eligibility criteria.
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of any adaptations is reported in the provided evidence.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms is present in the provided evidence.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence contains no description of any validation of the search strategy or validation studies/process.
There is no description of any peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) in the provided evidence.
The evidence does not state whether the search structure was non-PICO nor provide any description of a final conceptual structure or explorations used to develop it.

elements.quote: Two authors (EEN and JF) independently screened relevant trials. Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: The number of reviewers is reported for title/abstract screening (two authors) and for data extraction (six authors in pairs), but the evidence does not explicitly state the number of reviewers used for full-text eligibility screening stage distinct from extraction/risk-of-bias assessment, so reporting across all screening stages is incomplete.

elements.quote: Two authors (EEN and JF) independently screened relevant trials. Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that screening and data extraction were performed independently by the named reviewers.

elements.quote: Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion, or if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for resolving disagreements, with discussion and escalation to a third author if needed.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The authors report that they contacted trial authors to obtain or clarify eligibility/relevant data, describing the process used to obtain missing information from investigators.
No text in the provided evidence describes methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.
No information is provided about the use or integration of automation tools in the selection process.
There is no mention of externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed prior to screening in the supplied evidence.
No evidence describes internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use.
No information is provided about machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
The supplied evidence contains no description of crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection.
There is no mention of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived in the provided text.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number and grouping of reviewers who extracted data (six authors working in pairs).

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that data extraction was performed independently by the named pairs of authors.

elements.quote: Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion, or if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for resolving disagreements between data collectors, including escalation to a third author.

elements.quote: We contacted all trial authors if relevant data were unclear or missing.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that trial authors were contacted to obtain or clarify unclear/missing data.
No information about use, training, or validation of automation tools for data collection is reported in the provided evidence.
The provided evidence does not report any methods used to translate articles for data collection.
No information is provided about software used to extract data from figures in the retrieved evidence.
The manuscript does not describe decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or procedures for resolving inconsistencies between reported information in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Primary and secondary outcomes were predefined in our protocol [9]. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. We classified nonserious adverse events as any adverse event not assessed as serious according to the ICH-GCP definition.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists primary and secondary outcome domains and provides definitions for serious and nonserious adverse events.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: The time frame of measurement for outcomes is specified as the trial results at maximum follow-up.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: The manuscript states they used results at maximum follow-up (indicating a selection rule), but does not explicitly state whether they sought all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, all time points, all analyses) prior to applying that selection.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: A clear process for selecting results is described: when multiple results exist, the trial result at maximum follow-up was used.

elements.quote: Further, we included 'time to clinical improvement' as an outcome post hoc.
elements.reason: A change to outcomes (addition of a post hoc outcome) is reported, but no rationale for this change is provided in the cited text.
No evidence was provided describing changes to the processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or any rationale for such changes.

elements.quote: We assessed a total of 2 primary outcomes, and we therefore adjusted our thresholds for significance [18] and considered a p -value of 0.033 or less as the threshold for statistical significance [9,18]. Because we primarily considered results of secondary outcomes as hypothesis generating, we did not adjust the p -value for secondary outcomes.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies the two primary outcomes and describes adjusting significance thresholds and treating secondary outcomes as hypothesis-generating, which indicates prioritisation, but it does not explicitly state a broader rationale for why these outcomes were deemed most important beyond statistical adjustment.

elements.quote: Primary and secondary outcomes were predefined in our protocol [9]. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. We classified nonserious adverse events as any adverse event not assessed as serious according to the ICH-GCP definition.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists and defines the primary and secondary outcome variables and provides a definition for nonserious adverse events; other trial characteristics (e.g. follow-up time, inclusion criteria) are described elsewhere (text_15).

No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information was provided; the manuscript reports contacting trial authors for unclear or missing data but does not state any assumptions applied when data remained missing.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently extracted data using a standardized data extraction sheet.
elements.reason: A 'standardized data extraction sheet' is mentioned but no citation or named tool for determining which data items to collect is provided; thus there is no cited tool.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15].
elements.reason: The specific tool and version (Cochrane RoB 2) used to assess risk of bias is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Bias was assessed with the following domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from the intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of outcomes, and bias arising from selective reporting of results [12,15].
elements.reason: The domains/components assessed by the risk-of-bias tool are listed verbatim.

elements.quote: All trials were assessed as at high risk of bias ( S3 Table ).
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement (all trials high risk) is reported, but no rules or criteria used to derive the overall judgement are described in the provided evidence.
No description of adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool is present in the retrieved evidence.
No information about any newly developed risk-of-bias tool or its accessibility is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently assessed risk of bias. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: The number of reviewers (six, working in pairs), that they assessed independently, and the procedure for resolving disagreements (discussion or third author) are all described.

elements.quote: We contacted authors of trials with unclear or missing data.
elements.reason: The process to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study investigators (contacting trial authors for unclear/missing data) is explicitly stated.

elements.quote: Wehave identified 4 important reviews that are comparable to our present project [77-80]. The first is a network meta-analysis just published in BMJ [77]. However, at the time of publication, this project did not include all relevant trials [50,52,54-56,59-61,64], including the pivotal trials assessing the effects of hydroxychloroquine [54,55,59]. The second project is a literature review published in JAMA using PubMed to identify relevant English-language articles published through March 25, 2020, on pharmacological interventions for COVID-19. The search resulted in 1,315 total articles. This is because the authors also included case reports, case series, and review articles if they lacked randomised clinical trials. Moreover, this review was only a narrative review without meta-analytic methods and trial sequential analysis [78]. The third project is a living mapping of ongoing randomized clinical trials with network meta-analysis on all interventions for COVID-19. The authors are producing and disseminating preliminary results through an open platform [79]. This review includes both prevention and treatment and does not use trial sequential analysis or similar methods to handle problems with multiplicity (repeating updating of meta-analysis, multiple comparisons due to inclusion of multiple interventions, assessing multiple outcomes) [9]. The fourth project is a preprint of a rapid review assessing the effectiveness and safety of antiviral antibody treatments for COVID-19 published in medrXiv [80]. Fifty-four studies were included in the review: 3 controlled trials, 10 cohort studies, 7 retrospective medical record/database studies, and 34 case reports or series. These studies included patients with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS, n = 33), Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS, n = 16), COVID-19 ( n = 3), and unspecified coronavirus (n = 2). The most common treatment was ribavirin ( n = 41), followed by oseltamivir ( n = 10), and the combination of lopinavir/ritonavir ( n = 7). The authors conclude that current evidence for the effectiveness and safety of antiviral therapies for COVID-19 is inconclusive and suffers from a lack of well-designed prospective trials. Moreover, this review was only a narrative review without meta-analytic methods and trial sequential analysis [9].
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review's findings to four other relevant reviews, notes differences in included trials and methods, and places the results in the broader evidence context.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review also has limitations. Third, it was not possible to perform the planned individual patient data meta-analyses, network-meta-analysis, or the planned subgroup analyses because of the lack of relevant data. Fifth, all trials differed in the included participants' disease severity at trial intake (mild, moderate, severe, critically ill), which might result in clinical heterogeneity. We will explore disease severity as a subgroup analysis if this is warranted in later stages of this living systematic review. Sixth, the included trials assessed the outcomes at different time points, which might contribute to increased heterogeneity. Seventh, some data are included from preprints, and these might be subject to change following peer review. Therefore, some results, bias risk assessments, and GRADE summaries might change in later editions of this living systematic review following inclusion of the published peer-reviewed manuscripts.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly lists multiple limitations of the included evidence (paucity of trials, high risk of bias across trials, inability to perform planned analyses due to lack of data, heterogeneity in severity and time points, use of preprints, and a post hoc outcome), directly addressing limitations of the evidence included in the review.
